domains.title: Security, Compliance, and Governance for AI Solutions

articles.title: Choosing compute for containers on AWS: ECS vs EKS vs Fargate vs ECS Express Mode vs Lambda
articles.scope: Contrasts AWS container options by control-plane ownership, capacity model (Fargate, Fargate Spot, EC2, ECS Managed Instances, EKS Auto Mode), networking, identity and cost. Explains that App Runner closed to new customers on 2026-04-30 in favour of ECS Express Mode, and positions Lambda Web Functions (Node.js only) as the scale-to-zero HTTP alternative. Rates each option against Azure Container Apps, AKS and ACI. ECS and Express Mode are only partial matches for Container Apps because they lack scale to zero, KEDA and Dapr. Afterwards the reader can justify a platform choice for a .NET or Python service in an exam scenario or ADR.

articles.title: Amazon ECS in depth: task definitions, services, capacity providers, health checks, auto scaling, Service Connect and ECS Exec
articles.scope: Explains the ECS object model (cluster, task definition, task, service) and launch types versus capacity provider strategies. Covers awsvpc networking, container health checks and health-check grace periods, and service auto scaling through Application Auto Scaling target-tracking and step policies. Also covers Service Connect, the documented App Mesh successor for ECS workloads (App Mesh support ended 2026-09-30), and ECS Exec. Shows the same Fargate service in CDK (C#, Python), CloudFormation and Terraform. Afterwards the reader can build, scale and troubleshoot an ECS service end to end.

articles.title: Amazon EKS: what AWS adds to Kubernetes (Auto Mode, Pod Identity, access entries, VPC CNI, Load Balancer Controller, EKS Capabilities)
articles.scope: Builds on devops/kubernetes and covers only the AWS layer. That includes the managed control plane and upgrade cadence; managed node groups vs Fargate vs Karpenter vs EKS Auto Mode; VPC CNI IP management and prefix delegation; the AWS Load Balancer Controller; and CSI drivers. It also covers access entries, which replace the aws-auth ConfigMap, and EKS Capabilities (managed Argo CD, ACK, kro). Explains the service-mesh exit for EKS now that App Mesh has ended: Amazon VPC Lattice or an open-source mesh (verify current AWS guidance). Contrasts each feature with AKS. Afterwards the reader can design and operate a production EKS cluster.

articles.title: Container identity on AWS: ECS task role vs task execution role vs EKS Pod Identity vs IRSA
articles.scope: Separates the identity the platform uses to start a container (the task execution role) from the identity application code uses at runtime (the task role, Pod Identity or IRSA). Compares Pod Identity with IRSA on trust setup, token flow, session tags and cross-account access. Rates fidelity honestly. IRSA and Microsoft Entra Workload ID are a close match, because both federate a projected service-account token over OIDC. Pod Identity gets the same result through an EKS association API and a node agent, so it is only a partial match. Afterwards the reader can write least-privilege policies for each case and diagnose AccessDenied errors; the vendor-neutral concept stays in security/iam/workload-identity.

articles.title: Releasing containers on ECS and EKS: rolling updates with circuit breaker, built-in blue/green, linear and canary, CodeDeploy, and Argo CD
articles.scope: Covers implementation steps only; strategy definitions live in deployment-strategies-on-aws. Topics: ECS deployment controllers; the deployment circuit breaker and CloudWatch alarm-based rollback; and the 2025 built-in blue/green, linear and canary strategies with lifecycle hooks and test listeners. Also covers the CodeDeploy-based ECS blue/green that exam guides still describe, and GitOps on EKS with the managed Argo CD capability. Afterwards the reader can implement and roll back a container release in CDK, CloudFormation and Terraform.

articles.title: Amazon ECR operations: repositories, lifecycle policies, replication, pull-through cache, repository creation templates and cross-account pulls
articles.scope: Covers private repositories and ECR Public, repository policies for cross-account and cross-Region pulls, lifecycle rules, tag immutability, replication, pull-through cache for upstream registries and repository creation templates. Shows pushing images from CodeBuild or GitHub Actions through OIDC. Only summarizes basic vs enhanced (Inspector) scanning and managed signing; the security depth is in software-supply-chain-on-aws. Compares ECR with Azure Container Registry. Afterwards the reader can run a clean, cost-controlled registry for many teams.

articles.title: Hybrid and portable containers: ECS Anywhere vs EKS Anywhere vs EKS Hybrid Nodes vs EKS on Outposts vs EKS Distro vs ROSA
articles.scope: Contrasts where the control plane and the nodes run, connectivity and node-credential requirements (SSM activations, IAM Roles Anywhere), support and licensing models, and feature gaps such as load balancing for external instances. Rates fidelity against Azure. ROSA and Azure Red Hat OpenShift are an exact match; the other options map only partially to Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes and AKS on Azure Local. Afterwards the reader can choose a hybrid container option for data-residency, edge or migration scenarios.

articles.title: Containerizing and modernizing .NET workloads on AWS: AWS Transform for .NET, App2Container, Windows vs Linux containers on ECS and EKS
articles.scope: Takes a .NET Framework or ASP.NET Core application through four steps: assessment; porting to cross-platform .NET with AWS Transform for .NET; containerizing with a hand-written Dockerfile or App2Container (closed to new customers on 2025-11-07, still in DOP-C02 scope); and choosing Linux or Windows containers on ECS (Fargate or EC2) or EKS. The platform choice covers image size, licensing and gMSA trade-offs. Links architecture/migration for the 7 Rs and notes that AWS Migration Hub also closed to new customers on 2025-11-07 in favour of AWS Transform. Afterwards the reader can plan a .NET replatforming to containers and defend each step.

articles.title: Case study: moving the library's reference stack (.NET, Angular, Redis Streams, TimescaleDB, Docker Compose, MCP servers) to AWS
articles.scope: Maps each component of the reader's stack to AWS with fidelity notes. Docker Compose moves to ECS Express Mode or Fargate services, Redis Streams to ElastiCache for Valkey or MemoryDB, and TimescaleDB to the options in time-series-on-aws-for-timescaledb-users. SignalR maps to API Gateway WebSocket or AppSync Events, the Angular front end to Amplify Hosting or S3 with CloudFront, and the MCP servers to Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and Gateway (depth in ai/platforms). Ends with an ADR-style summary of cost, risk and effort. Afterwards the reader can execute and defend an end-to-end migration plan.

articles.title: Lambda Event Functions execution model: invocation types, concurrency, scaling, cold starts, SnapStart and the runtime lifecycle
articles.scope: Explains the execution environment lifecycle and the three invocation types (synchronous, asynchronous, event source mapping). Covers reserved vs provisioned concurrency, scaling rates, memory and CPU tuning, VPC access, extensions and SnapStart for .NET and Python, mapped to Azure Functions hosting plans. A runtime-lifecycle section gives the dates this reader needs: dotnet8 is deprecated on 2026-11-10 with dotnet10 current, dotnet9 is container-image only, python3.10 is deprecated on 2026-10-31, and Amazon Linux 2 reached end of life on 2026-06-30. Managed runtimes exist only for LTS releases, so STS versions need a container image or Native AOT on provided.al2023. Afterwards the reader can tune a function for latency, cost and quotas and plan runtime upgrades.

articles.title: Packaging, versioning and releasing Lambda Event Functions for .NET and Python: zip vs container image, layers, versions and aliases, Native AOT, SnapStart and code signing
articles.scope: Compares .zip and container-image packages on size limits, layers, base images and cold start. Builds .NET with Native AOT and Python with dependency layers. Publishes immutable versions behind aliases, using weighted routing for canary releases and instant rollback. Shows SnapStart and provisioned concurrency on aliases, per-environment configuration, and code signing configurations (signing depth is in software-supply-chain-on-aws). Afterwards the reader can ship and roll back a function safely in SAM, CDK and Terraform.

articles.title: Lambda failure handling: retries, destinations, DLQs, partial batch responses and idempotency
articles.scope: Shows how retry behaviour differs by invocation type and when to use destinations vs DLQs. Covers ReportBatchItemFailures for SQS and Kinesis, the bisect and maximum-age settings, and Powertools idempotency in C# and Python. Links messaging/eventing/delivery-semantics and messaging/eventing/outbox-pattern. Afterwards the reader can make an event-driven function safe under at-least-once delivery.

articles.title: The Lambda compute family: Event Functions vs Web Functions vs MicroVMs vs Managed Instances vs durable functions, and when to leave for Step Functions, ECS Express Mode or AgentCore Runtime
articles.scope: Contrasts the five options on programming model, duration, concurrency, isolation, scaling and pricing. Durations range from 15 minutes per invocation, to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations on Managed Instances, 8 hours per MicroVM, and one year per durable execution. Isolation is Firecracker or, on Managed Instances, Nitro containers; Managed Instances add a 15% fee to EC2 prices, and Web Functions bill active CPU plus environment memory. Notes the language limits: Web Functions are Node.js only, while Managed Instances support Java 21+, Python 3.13+, Node.js 22+, .NET 8+ and Rust. Rates Azure counterparts: Durable Functions (close), Container Apps dynamic sessions for MicroVMs (close), and Container Apps or Flex Consumption for Web Functions (partial). Afterwards the reader can pick an execution model for steady-state, long-running, HTTP, sandboxed or human-in-the-loop work. Exam refs apply to the Event Functions and Step Functions content only; the newer options are beyond current exam guides.

articles.title: API front doors on AWS: API Gateway REST vs HTTP vs WebSocket APIs vs AppSync GraphQL and Events vs Lambda function URLs
articles.scope: Compares API types by features (authorizers, usage plans, caching, validation, WAF, private endpoints), latency, price and real-time model. Covers stages, custom domains and throttling, with function URLs and Web Functions endpoints as the minimal options. Rates Azure counterparts. REST APIs match API Management closely. WebSocket APIs match Web PubSub only partially: they have no groups or broadcast, so the backend iterates @connections. AppSync Events matches Web PubSub closely. Links messaging/apis/rest-vs-grpc-apis and messaging/realtime/signalr-websockets. Afterwards the reader can design, secure and version an API for an Angular front end.

articles.title: API Gateway integrations and transformations: proxy vs non-proxy, mapping templates, request validation, gateway responses, mock integrations and cache keys
articles.scope: Shows Lambda proxy vs custom integrations, HTTP and AWS service integrations, and VTL mapping templates for request and response transformation and status-code overrides. Also covers request validators and models, gateway responses, MOCK integrations for contract-first testing, stage variables per environment, and caching keyed on headers, query strings and paths. Afterwards the reader can implement and debug the API Gateway behaviours DVA-C02 tests.

articles.title: Choosing AWS messaging: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis vs MSK vs Amazon MQ
articles.scope: A decision guide that contrasts queues, pub/sub topics, event buses, streams and brokers on delivery semantics, ordering, retention, replay, fan-out, throughput and cost. Links messaging/eventing/event-driven-vs-request-response and messaging/eventing/redis-streams-vs-kafka. Keeps only a pointer table to Azure Service Bus, Event Grid and Event Hubs; the cross-cloud discussion lives in cloud/compare. Afterwards the reader can pick and defend an integration service in exam scenarios.

articles.title: Amazon SQS and SNS in depth: standard vs FIFO vs fair queues, visibility timeout, long polling, DLQs, fan-out and filtering
articles.scope: For SQS, details short and long polling, visibility timeout, delay queues, DLQ redrive, FIFO message groups and deduplication, fair queues for noisy-neighbour isolation, the 1 MiB message limit and the Extended Client for larger payloads. For SNS, covers standard and FIFO topics, filter policies, raw delivery and SNS-to-SQS fan-out. Includes C# and Python producers and consumers. Afterwards the reader can build reliable queue-based decoupling and debug stuck or duplicate messages.

articles.title: Amazon EventBridge: event buses, rules and patterns, archive and replay, schema registry, Pipes, Scheduler and cross-account routing
articles.scope: Explains default, custom and partner buses, event patterns and input transformers, target retries and DLQs, and API destinations. Also covers archive and replay, the schema registry and discovery, global endpoints, Pipes, EventBridge Scheduler (a separate capability from scheduled rules) and AWS service events as operational triggers. Maps to Azure Event Grid. Afterwards the reader can implement event-driven integrations and operational automations and troubleshoot rules that do not match.

articles.title: AWS Step Functions: Standard vs Express, integration patterns, JSONata and variables, Distributed Map, error handling and human approval
articles.scope: Covers Amazon States Language and Standard vs Express semantics and pricing. Explains the request-response, .sync and .waitForTaskToken integration patterns, Distributed Map over large S3 datasets, Retry and Catch, variables and JSONata, and the TestState API. Includes human approval steps, such as approving AI-driven operations (an SAP-C02 emerging topic). Shows the AWS implementation only and links architecture/patterns for saga theory. Afterwards the reader can model an orchestrated workflow with compensation and deploy it with SAM or CDK.

articles.title: Streaming on AWS: Kinesis Data Streams vs Amazon Data Firehose vs Amazon MSK vs Managed Service for Apache Flink
articles.scope: For Kinesis Data Streams, contrasts shards and capacity modes, partition keys, retention and replay, and enhanced fan-out with KCL consumers. For Firehose, covers buffering, transformation and format conversion. For MSK, compares provisioned clusters (Standard and Express brokers) with Serverless. Covers Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) and the discontinuation of the legacy SQL applications: no new apps from 2025-10-15, deletion from 2026-01-27. Flags Kinesis Video Streams as a media service rather than a data stream, and maps to Azure Event Hubs and Stream Analytics. Afterwards the reader can design and size an ingestion pipeline.

articles.title: In-memory data on AWS: ElastiCache (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached) vs MemoryDB vs DAX, and caching strategies
articles.scope: Explains serverless vs node-based ElastiCache, cluster mode, replication and Global Datastore. Covers MemoryDB durability, DAX for DynamoDB, and lazy loading vs write-through with TTLs and session stores. Links messaging/eventing/redis-streams-vs-kafka and maps to Azure Managed Redis. Afterwards the reader can add a cache to a .NET or Python app and choose the right in-memory service.

articles.title: Serverless integration patterns on AWS: SNS-to-SQS fan-out, claim check with the SQS Extended Client, choreography with EventBridge vs orchestration with Step Functions, idempotent consumers, retries and circuit breakers
articles.scope: Implements each pattern with AWS services and C# and Python code, and links architecture/patterns for the theory. Shows where each pattern's failure modes appear: poison messages, retry storms and duplicate delivery. Covers SDK retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers in application code and Powertools idempotency. Afterwards the reader can choose and implement the right integration pattern in exam scenarios and production designs.

articles.title: Notifications and customer messaging on AWS: SNS (SMS and mobile push) vs Amazon SES vs AWS End User Messaging vs Amazon Connect
articles.scope: Separates application-to-application fan-out from application-to-person channels. Covers email with SES (identities, DKIM, configuration sets, bounce handling), SNS SMS and mobile push, and SMS, voice, push and WhatsApp with AWS End User Messaging. End User Messaging carries Amazon Pinpoint's channels forward; Pinpoint reaches end of support on 2026-10-30. Amazon Connect appears only as a contact-centre orientation. Maps to Azure Communication Services and Notification Hubs. Afterwards the reader can pick a channel service and migrate Pinpoint-era designs.

articles.title: Brokers and SaaS integration on AWS: Amazon MQ (ActiveMQ, RabbitMQ) vs Amazon AppFlow vs EventBridge partner event sources and API destinations
articles.scope: Explains when to lift and shift an existing JMS, AMQP, MQTT or STOMP broker to Amazon MQ instead of re-architecting onto SQS and SNS. Shows how AppFlow moves data between SaaS applications and AWS on a schedule or on events, and how partner event sources and API destinations connect EventBridge to SaaS. Links messaging/integration/broker-exchange-api-integrations and maps to Azure Service Bus, Logic Apps connectors and Event Grid partner topics. Afterwards the reader can answer broker-migration and SaaS-integration scenarios.

articles.title: Amazon S3 storage classes, Intelligent-Tiering and lifecycle rules
articles.scope: Compares every storage class by AZ resilience, availability, minimum duration, minimum billable size and retrieval model. Explains Intelligent-Tiering's access tiers and its per-object monitoring fee. Covers lifecycle transitions and expirations, including noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads, and notes that the legacy vault-based Amazon Glacier service closed to new customers on 2025-12-15. Maps to Azure Blob access tiers and lifecycle management. Afterwards the reader can design a cost-optimal tiering policy and quantify its trade-offs.

articles.title: Protecting S3 data: versioning, Object Lock, replication, Block Public Access, Object Ownership and encryption
articles.scope: Shows how these controls combine into defence in depth: versioning, MFA Delete, Object Lock modes and legal holds, CRR and SRR with Replication Time Control and Batch Replication, Block Public Access, Object Ownership, bucket policies, and SSE-S3, SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS with S3 Bucket Keys. Explains that since April 2026 SSE-C is blocked by default through the BlockedEncryptionTypes setting, and that blocked requests return 403 AccessDenied. The block covers new general purpose buckets and existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C objects, and the page explains why that helps against ransomware. Snippets are in CloudFormation, Terraform and the Bicep equivalent for Azure Storage. Afterwards the reader can harden a bucket for compliance and ransomware resilience.

articles.title: S3 access and performance patterns: bucket policies vs access points, presigned URLs, multipart upload, Transfer Acceleration, event notifications, Express One Zone, Mountpoint and S3 Files
articles.scope: Covers how S3 evaluates request authorization; access points and Multi-Region Access Points; presigned URLs from C# and Python; and multipart uploads and per-prefix request rates. Also covers Transfer Acceleration, Requester Pays, S3 Event Notifications vs the EventBridge integration, Batch Operations, and Express One Zone directory buckets. Ends with Mountpoint for Amazon S3 and the April 2026 S3 Files NFS mount for EC2, Lambda, ECS and EKS. Afterwards the reader can implement secure direct-to-S3 uploads from an Angular client and tune throughput.

articles.title: Block vs file storage on AWS: EBS volume types and snapshots vs EFS vs the FSx family vs S3 Files
articles.scope: For EBS, compares gp3, io2 Block Express, st1 and sc1 performance and cost, and covers Elastic Volumes changes, troubleshooting with EBS performance metrics, and instance store. Snapshot topics include automation with Data Lifecycle Manager vs AWS Backup, Fast Snapshot Restore and Recycle Bin. Also covers EFS throughput modes and storage classes, and FSx for Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS, with their backups, snapshots and shadow copies. Maps to Azure Managed Disks, Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files and Azure Managed Lustre. Afterwards the reader can choose, protect and tune block or shared storage for a workload.

articles.title: AWS Backup and data-layer recovery: backup plans, Vault Lock, logically air-gapped vaults, restore testing and Elastic Disaster Recovery
articles.scope: Centralizes backups with Organizations backup policies and cross-Region and cross-account copies. Protects them with Vault Lock, logically air-gapped vaults, restore testing, Backup Audit Manager and GuardDuty Malware Protection for AWS Backup. Layers Elastic Disaster Recovery for servers on top, against RTO and RPO targets defined in architecture/reliability. Afterwards the reader can design and evidence a ransomware-resilient backup strategy.

articles.title: Amazon RDS vs Aurora: Multi-AZ instance vs Multi-AZ cluster vs Aurora cluster, replicas, RDS Proxy, Serverless v2, Global Database and Blue/Green Deployments
articles.scope: Contrasts storage architecture, failover behaviour and time, replica types and endpoints, and Aurora replica auto scaling. Also covers RDS Proxy, IAM database authentication, storage autoscaling, Blue/Green Deployments, backups and PITR, Aurora Serverless v2, I/O-Optimized pricing, and Global Database switchover vs failover. RDS Custom and SQL Server options have their own article. Notes that CLOUDOPS-A skill 1.3.5 still says Performance Insights for what the console now calls CloudWatch Database Insights. Maps to Azure Database flexible server, Azure SQL and Azure HorizonDB (preview). Afterwards the reader can choose and operate the right relational option for HA, DR and cost.

articles.title: DynamoDB for developers: keys, GSIs vs LSIs, query vs scan, consistency, capacity modes, table classes and transactions
articles.scope: Teaches access-pattern-first modelling, high-cardinality partition keys, single-table design and the trade-offs between GSIs and LSIs. Covers query vs scan, strongly vs eventually consistent reads, condition expressions and optimistic locking, transactions, TTL, table classes, and on-demand vs provisioned capacity, with C# and Python SDK code. Maps to Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Afterwards the reader can model and implement a table for real access patterns.

articles.title: DynamoDB at scale: Streams, global tables (MREC vs MRSC) vs Aurora DSQL, PITR and backups
articles.scope: Covers change data capture with DynamoDB Streams vs Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, and Lambda triggers. Explains global table consistency modes, multi-account replicas and last-writer-wins conflicts, along with PITR with configurable recovery periods and export to S3. Shows when Aurora DSQL's active-active, strongly consistent SQL is the better multi-Region choice. Afterwards the reader can design a multi-Region, event-driven data architecture with a known RPO and consistency model.

articles.title: Purpose-built databases on AWS: DocumentDB, Keyspaces, Neptune, Timestream and Aurora DSQL, and when not to use them
articles.scope: A selection reference that maps data models and access patterns to AWS engines. Notes compatibility limits (DocumentDB vs MongoDB, Keyspaces vs Cassandra), scaling models and status changes, such as Timestream for LiveAnalytics being closed to new customers. OpenSearch Service has its own article. Links the data/ articles and maps each engine to its Azure counterpart. Afterwards the reader can quickly shortlist a database for a stated requirement.

articles.title: The AWS analytics stack: S3 data lake, Glue, Athena, Lake Formation, EMR, Redshift, S3 Tables and Amazon Quick Sight
articles.scope: Orients across ingestion, cataloguing, governance, querying and warehousing. Covers the Glue Data Catalog, crawlers and jobs; Athena partitioning and columnar formats; and Lake Formation permissions with LF-Tags vs IAM. Also covers EMR on EC2, EKS and Serverless; Redshift Serverless and zero-ETL integrations; S3 Tables for Apache Iceberg; AWS Data Exchange; and Amazon Quick Sight (formerly QuickSight). Lakehouse and data-mesh concepts stay in architecture/data-architecture; links data/time-series/row-vs-columnar-storage. Afterwards the reader can design a secure, cost-aware data lake.

articles.title: Moving data into AWS: DMS and Schema Conversion vs DataSync vs Transfer Family vs Storage Gateway vs Data Transfer Terminal and the Snow Family
articles.scope: Compares online and offline transfer options by data type, bandwidth, cutover and security. The options are DMS full load plus CDC, DMS Schema Conversion and AWS SCT, DataSync, Transfer Family, and the Storage Gateway types (FSx File Gateway is no longer available to new customers). Physical options are covered now that Snowball Edge is closed to new customers. Links architecture/migration for strategy. Afterwards the reader can choose the fastest compliant transfer mechanism in migration scenarios.

articles.title: Running SQL Server and .NET data tiers on AWS: RDS for SQL Server vs RDS Custom vs SQL Server on EC2 vs Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL
articles.scope: Compares the four options on control, HA (Multi-AZ, or Always On availability groups on EC2), licensing, cost and migration effort. Licensing covers License Included vs BYOL with Dedicated Hosts or License Mobility. Includes Babelfish's T-SQL and TDS compatibility gaps and what they mean for Entity Framework Core. Maps to Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure VMs. Afterwards the reader can choose and justify a data tier for a .NET workload in an SAP-C02 migration scenario.

articles.title: Time-series on AWS for a TimescaleDB user: RDS and Aurora PostgreSQL without the timescaledb extension vs Timestream for InfluxDB vs self-managed or Marketplace TimescaleDB
articles.scope: Starts from the reader's TimescaleDB design (hypertables, continuous aggregates, compression) and maps each feature onto AWS options: native PostgreSQL partitioning on RDS or Aurora, Timestream for InfluxDB, and TimescaleDB on EC2 or through AWS Marketplace. Timestream for LiveAnalytics is closed to new customers. The point of the page is the fidelity gap against Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, which offers a TimescaleDB extension; verify both providers' current extension lists before writing. Links data/time-series/time-series-financial-schemas. Afterwards the reader can choose a time-series store on AWS knowing what is lost.

articles.title: Multi-tenant data isolation on AWS: dynamodb:LeadingKeys, ABAC with session tags, Aurora PostgreSQL row-level security, per-tenant S3 access points and KMS keys
articles.scope: Implements silo, pool and bridge isolation at the data layer; the theory is in architecture/patterns. The mechanisms are dynamodb:LeadingKeys fine-grained access, ABAC with STS session tags, Aurora PostgreSQL row-level security, per-tenant S3 access points and prefixes, and per-tenant KMS keys or encryption context. Shows how tenant context travels from a .NET or Python API through the token to IAM conditions, and how to test for cross-tenant leakage. Afterwards the reader can design and defend tenant isolation for a SaaS data tier.

articles.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service for search, logs and vectors: managed domains vs Serverless, OpenSearch Ingestion, direct query and zero-ETL, S3 Vectors offload
articles.scope: Explains managed domains (instance types, shards, UltraWarm and cold storage, Multi-AZ with standby) vs Serverless collections. Covers OpenSearch Ingestion pipelines, direct query over S3 and CloudWatch Logs, zero-ETL from DynamoDB, fine-grained access control, and OpenSearch as a log destination from CloudWatch Logs and Firehose. Treats the vector engine and S3 Vectors offload at storage depth only; vector-store selection for RAG stays in ai/platforms. Afterwards the reader can size, secure and feed an OpenSearch workload.

articles.title: CloudWatch metrics and alarms: namespaces, dimensions, resolution, OpenTelemetry vs Classic metrics, EMF, metric math, composite and anomaly-detection alarms, and alarm actions
articles.scope: Explains metric identity and resolution; custom metrics through PutMetricData, OTLP and EMF; PromQL on OpenTelemetry metrics; and metric math. Covers alarm evaluation (M of N, missing data), composite and anomaly-detection alarms, and every alarm action: SNS, EC2, Auto Scaling, Systems Manager OpsItems, Lambda, EventBridge state-change events and starting a CloudWatch investigation. Maps to Azure Monitor metrics and alert rules. Afterwards the reader can instrument and alert on a service without alarm noise.

articles.title: CloudWatch Logs: log groups, retention and classes, data protection, metric and subscription filters, Logs Insights, Live Tail and anomaly detection
articles.scope: Shows structured logging from .NET and Python, retention and the Infrequent Access class, and KMS encryption with data-protection masking of sensitive fields. Contrasts metric filters with subscription filters, and covers cross-account centralization. Writes Logs Insights queries in its own language, SQL and PPL, and covers Live Tail, log anomaly detection and the cost levers of log classes and retention. Maps to Log Analytics and KQL. Afterwards the reader can build a logging pipeline and answer production questions with queries.

articles.title: Tracing on AWS: X-Ray vs ADOT and OpenTelemetry, Transaction Search and Application Signals
articles.scope: Explains traces, segments, subsegments, annotations vs metadata, and sampling. Migrates from the X-Ray SDKs and daemon (in maintenance mode since 2026-02-25, end of support 2027-02-25) to OpenTelemetry and ADOT for Lambda, ECS, EKS and API Gateway, with the CloudWatch agent replacing the daemon. Includes the mapping DVA-C02 depends on: OpenTelemetry span attributes become X-Ray metadata unless listed in aws.xray.annotations. Then enables Application Signals and Transaction Search; SLO concepts stay in devops/sre. Afterwards the reader can trace a distributed .NET or Python request end to end.

articles.title: CloudTrail vs CloudWatch vs AWS Config: who did what, how is it behaving, how is it configured
articles.scope: Separates three kinds of evidence. Audit comes from CloudTrail: management, data, network activity and Insights events, trails and organization trails, and Event history; CloudTrail Lake closed to new customers on 2026-05-31. Telemetry comes from CloudWatch, and configuration state from AWS Config (owned by cloud/aws/governance). Maps to Azure Activity Log, Azure Monitor and Resource Graph. Afterwards the reader can choose the right evidence source for audit, troubleshooting and compliance questions.

articles.title: Observability at organization scale: cross-account observability, log centralization, metric streams, Managed Prometheus and Grafana, Synthetics and RUM, and the cost of telemetry
articles.scope: Designs a central monitoring account with cross-account observability links and log centralization. Adds CloudWatch metric streams to Firehose or partners, Managed Service for Prometheus and Managed Grafana for containers, and Synthetics canaries and RUM for an Angular front end. Prepares for investigations with CloudWatch investigation groups and AWS Health events linked from cloud/aws/governance. Treats telemetry cost as a design input: log classes, retention, metric cardinality and data transfer. Afterwards the reader can propose and defend a multi-account observability architecture.

articles.title: CloudWatch's Insights family compared: Container Insights vs Lambda Insights vs Database Insights vs Contributor Insights vs Application Signals vs CloudWatch Network Monitoring
articles.scope: Contrasts what each feature collects, how it is enabled (agent, extension layer, console toggle or rule), its cost model and the questions it answers. Database Insights is the current name for what CLOUDOPS-A skill 1.3.5 calls Performance Insights. Network Monitoring comprises Internet Monitor, Network Flow Monitor and Network Synthetic Monitor. Maps each feature to its Azure Monitor counterpart: Container insights, Application Insights, VM insights or Network Watcher. Afterwards the reader can pick the right Insights tool for a symptom.

articles.title: AI agents for AWS operations and security: AWS DevOps Agent vs CloudWatch investigations vs CloudWatch Omni vs Continuum for penetration testing vs Kiro vs Amazon Q Developer
articles.scope: Contrasts what each tool investigates or produces, what triggers it (alarm, console, IDE or schedule), its permissions and data access, its level of autonomy, its audit trail and where human approval sits. Uses the names CLOUDOPS-A v1.1 tests (AWS DevOps Agent, AWS Security Agent, Kiro) alongside current product names. Maps to Azure SRE Agent, Microsoft Copilot in Azure, Microsoft Security Copilot and the GitHub Copilot coding agent. Links ai/applied for agentic-coding practice and security/ai-security for agent risk. Afterwards the reader can choose and govern AI assistance for operations and security work.

articles.title: AWS security services map: prevent, detect, investigate, respond and protect data
articles.scope: Places every AWS security service, including those owned by the identity, governance and networking folders, on a prevent, detect, investigate, respond and protect-data matrix. Each entry gives inputs, outputs, delegated-administrator support and the closest Microsoft service. The map includes AWS Continuum, AWS Security Incident Response, and the AI-governance services AIF-C01 names (Config, Inspector, Audit Manager, Artifact, CloudTrail, Trusted Advisor, Macie). Links security/cloud-security for vendor-neutral architecture. Afterwards the reader can eliminate distractors in service-selection questions.

articles.title: AWS KMS in depth: key types, key policies vs IAM vs grants, encryption context, envelope encryption, rotation, multi-Region keys and custom key stores
articles.scope: Explains customer managed vs AWS managed vs AWS owned keys, and symmetric, asymmetric and HMAC keys. Covers key policy evaluation (IAM policies apply only when the key policy delegates to the account), grants as a separate key-specific delegation mechanism, and encryption context with the kms:ViaService condition. Then covers GenerateDataKey envelope encryption, rotation options, multi-Region keys, imported key material, CloudHSM and external key stores, and cross-account use. Maps to Azure Key Vault and Managed HSM. Afterwards the reader can design key hierarchies and fix KMS AccessDenied errors.

articles.title: Secrets Manager vs Systems Manager Parameter Store, and secret injection into Lambda, ECS and EKS
articles.scope: Compares cost, rotation (managed or Lambda-based, single-user vs alternating-users), cross-Region replication, size and throughput limits, hierarchies and versioning. Shows injection through ECS secrets, the Lambda extension and the Secrets Store CSI driver, with client-side caching in C# and Python, and when configuration belongs in AppConfig instead. Maps to Azure Key Vault and App Configuration. Afterwards the reader can remove hard-coded credentials and automate rotation.

articles.title: Certificates and keys on AWS: ACM public, imported and exportable certificates, AWS Private CA, development certificates and SSH keys, and where TLS terminates
articles.scope: Covers DNS vs email validation, managed renewal and how it fails, the us-east-1 rule for CloudFront, expiry monitoring for imported certificates, and exportable public certificates. Also covers AWS Private CA's general-purpose and short-lived modes with mTLS, development certificates and EC2 key pairs (with Session Manager as the keyless alternative), and TLS termination on ALB, NLB, CloudFront and API Gateway. Notes that Azure has no first-party workload CA: Key Vault issues certificates through integrated or external CAs. Links security/iam/mtls-vs-api-keys. Afterwards the reader can implement and monitor encryption in transit.

articles.title: Threat detection and posture on AWS: GuardDuty vs Inspector vs Macie vs Security Hub vs Security Hub CSPM vs Detective vs Security Lake
articles.scope: Contrasts each service's data sources, finding types and formats (ASFF vs OCSF), and explains the December 2025 split into Security Hub and Security Hub CSPM. Covers GuardDuty protection plans, including AI Protection, Extended Threat Detection, Investigation (preview) and custom detection rules. Also covers Inspector scan types including code security and SBOM export, Macie discovery, Detective investigation and Security Lake, with AWS Security Incident Response as the triage layer on top. A legacy-wording box maps DOP-C02's 'Inspector assessment templates' (Inspector Classic) to continuous scanning. The Azure mapping is stack-to-service: together the AWS services are close to Microsoft Defender for Cloud, but each alone is only partial. Afterwards the reader can design a detection stack and route any finding to the right service.

articles.title: Automated security response on AWS: delegated administrators, EventBridge routing, automation rules, SSM remediation, Access Analyzer findings and Firewall Manager
articles.scope: Builds an organization-wide pattern: delegated administrator accounts, cross-Region aggregation, Security Hub automation rules and ticketing, and remediation from EventBridge to Lambda or Systems Manager Automation. Adds IAM Access Analyzer external, internal and unused access findings (policy generation stays in cloud/aws/identity) and Firewall Manager policies, with blast-radius controls and testing. Links security/detection-response. Afterwards the reader can implement and test automated remediation safely.

articles.title: Service-to-service authentication on AWS: SigV4 and IAM auth vs Cognito client credentials vs mTLS with AWS Private CA vs VPC Lattice auth policies vs IAM Roles Anywhere
articles.scope: Compares how microservices prove their identity to each other on AWS: trust anchor, credential lifetime, rotation, network dependency and where authorization happens. Shows where fine-grained application authorization with Amazon Verified Permissions (owned by cloud/aws/identity) fits. Includes C# and Python examples of SigV4 request signing and the client-credentials grant. Links security/iam/mtls-vs-api-keys and security/iam/workload-identity. Afterwards the reader can choose an authentication scheme for east-west traffic.

articles.title: Protecting sensitive data in application code: KMS-encrypted Lambda environment variables, AWS Encryption SDK vs AWS Database Encryption SDK vs S3 Encryption Client, log masking and Macie classification
articles.scope: Covers choosing client-side vs server-side encryption, and encrypting Lambda environment variables with a customer managed key that is decrypted at init. Shows envelope encryption with the AWS Encryption SDK, attribute-level encryption and searchable beacons with the AWS Database Encryption SDK (formerly the DynamoDB Encryption Client), and the S3 Encryption Client. Sanitizes and masks data with Powertools and CloudWatch Logs data protection, and uses Macie to classify whatever still leaks. Afterwards the reader can keep secrets and PII out of logs, configuration and databases in .NET and Python.

articles.title: Incident response on AWS: AWS Security Incident Response, containment runbooks for EC2, IAM and S3, forensic snapshots and the exposed-access-key playbook
articles.scope: Turns findings into response. Preparation covers roles, break-glass access and forensic accounts. AWS Security Incident Response triages GuardDuty and Security Hub CSPM findings, runs pre-authorized containment and publishes case events to EventBridge. The runbooks isolate EC2 instances and capture EBS snapshots and memory, revoke IAM sessions and rotate exposed access keys, and lock down exposed S3 buckets. Links security/detection-response for the vendor-neutral lifecycle and practice/tabletops for exercises. Afterwards the reader can run and document an AWS incident from detection to recovery.

articles.title: Software supply chain on AWS: ECR managed signing with AWS Signer, Lambda code signing, Inspector SBOM and code security, CodeArtifact package origin controls
articles.scope: Implements the AWS controls behind the concepts in security/supply-chain. Signs container images through ECR managed signing (AWS Signer, Notation) and verifies them at admission on EKS. Adds Lambda code signing configurations, ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector code security and SBOM export, CodeArtifact package origin controls against dependency confusion, and build provenance from CodeBuild. Afterwards the reader can build an end-to-end, verifiable pipeline from source to running workload.

articles.title: AWS CloudFormation in depth: templates, change sets, StackSets, drift, modules, Hooks, Guard, custom resources and rollback
articles.scope: Explains template anatomy, intrinsic functions, SSM parameter types and nested stacks vs modules. Covers change sets, rollback triggers and stack policies, DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy, and creation policies with cfn-signal and the other helper scripts. Then covers StackSets (self-managed and service-managed), drift detection, the IaC generator, custom resources, and Hooks with Guard rules, comparing each with ARM, Bicep and deployment stacks. Afterwards the reader can author, deploy and govern stacks across accounts and Regions.

articles.title: Choosing IaC for AWS: CloudFormation vs CDK vs SAM, with Terraform as the cross-cloud baseline
articles.scope: Contrasts authoring model, state handling, drift, testing, policy as code and multi-cloud reach. Shows one resource in CloudFormation, CDK (C# and Python), SAM and Terraform, and covers construct levels, bootstrapping and the CDK Toolkit Library. Notes that HashiCorp deprecated CDK for Terraform on 2025-12-10, and that Azure has no first-party CDK: Aspire's Azure provisioning, which generates Bicep, is a partial analogue and Pulumi is third-party. Links devops/iac and maps to Bicep. Afterwards the reader can write an IaC ADR for an AWS-only or dual-cloud team.

articles.title: AWS SAM for .NET and Python: templates, local testing, sam sync and gradual deployments
articles.scope: Walks through the AWS::Serverless transform, policy templates and connectors, sam build, local invoke and start-api, sam sync for fast iteration, and multiple environments. Covers DeploymentPreference for Lambda traffic shifting with alarms and hooks, and Infrastructure Composer for visual editing. Strategy definitions live in deployment-strategies-on-aws and testing depth in testing-serverless-and-event-driven-apps-on-aws. Afterwards the reader can develop and ship a serverless API the way DVA-C02 expects.

articles.title: CI/CD with AWS developer tools: CodePipeline V2, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CodeConnections and FIS gates
articles.scope: Builds a pipeline with Git triggers through CodeConnections, variables and execution modes, buildspec phases, reports and caching, and artifact and secret handling. Adds manual approvals, CodeDeploy AppSpec hooks and deployment configurations, cross-account deploy roles with KMS-encrypted artifacts, and Fault Injection Service experiments as quality gates. Shows GitHub Actions through OIDC as an alternative; package repositories are covered in artifact-repositories-codeartifact. Links devops/ci-cd-pipelines. Afterwards the reader can implement and debug a multi-account AWS pipeline.

articles.title: Deployment strategies on AWS: in-place vs rolling vs immutable vs blue/green vs canary and linear across EC2, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, Lambda and API Gateway
articles.scope: The hub for deployment strategy definitions on AWS. Maps in-place, rolling, rolling with an additional batch, immutable, blue/green, canary and linear to the mechanism on each platform: Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies, CodeDeploy configurations, ECS built-in strategies, Lambda alias weights, API Gateway canary stages and AppConfig gradual rollouts. Covers rollback triggers and data-migration caveats; Route 53 weighted records and health checks are linked from cloud/aws/networking. Builds on the neutral terms blue-green-deployment, canary-release and rolling-deployment. Afterwards the reader can pick the strategy that meets downtime, cost and risk constraints.

articles.title: AWS Systems Manager for operations: Session Manager, Run Command, State Manager, Inventory, Patch Manager, maintenance windows, Automation, OpsCenter and AppConfig
articles.scope: Explains managed nodes, SSM Agent and hybrid activations, and the unified console. Covers Session Manager vs SSH and bastions, Run Command vs State Manager, Inventory, and patch baselines with patch policies and maintenance windows. Also covers Automation runbooks triggered by EventBridge or Config remediation, OpsCenter (Incident Manager and Change Manager closed to new customers on 2025-11-07), and AppConfig feature flags. Maps to Azure Arc, Azure Automation and Azure Update Manager. Afterwards the reader can automate fleet operations without inbound access.

articles.title: AWS SDKs, CLI and developer tools for .NET and Python: credential chain, retries, pagination, waiters, Toolkit for Visual Studio, Q Developer and Kiro
articles.scope: Shows the default credential provider chain and profiles, SigV4, and retry modes with exponential backoff and jitter. Covers pagination, waiters and presigners in the AWS SDK for .NET and Boto3; CLI output and --query techniques; CloudShell; the AWS Toolkit for Visual Studio; and the AWS MCP servers that coding agents use. Treats Amazon Q Developer (IDE plugins reach end of support on 2027-04-30) and Kiro at exam depth only, marked as unscored emerging topics, and links ai/applied for agentic-coding practice. Afterwards the reader can write resilient SDK code that handles throttling correctly.

articles.title: Testing serverless and event-driven applications on AWS: unit tests with mocks, sam local and sam remote invoke, shareable test events, Step Functions TestState, integration tests in the cloud and AI-generated tests
articles.scope: Builds a test pyramid in C# and Python for Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions and EventBridge code. Layers run from unit tests with SDK mocks, sam local invoke and start-api, sam remote invoke with shareable test events, and Step Functions TestState up to integration tests in ephemeral cloud environments and contract tests with MOCK integrations. Adds load tests and coverage gates in pipelines. Treats AI-generated tests from Q Developer or Kiro as unscored emerging content. Afterwards the reader can design a test strategy that DVA-C02 and DOP-C02 scenarios reward.

articles.title: Troubleshooting failed deployments on AWS: CloudFormation stack and rollback failures, CodeBuild and CodeDeploy lifecycle errors, ECS stopped tasks and circuit breaker, EKS pending pods, subnet sizing and permission errors
articles.scope: A symptom-to-cause-to-fix reference for the states exam scenarios turn on. Covers CREATE_FAILED and UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED with continue-update-rollback, custom resources that never respond, CodeBuild phase failures, and CodeDeploy lifecycle hook timeouts and failed health checks. Also covers ECS stopped-task reasons and circuit-breaker rollbacks, EKS pods pending on IP exhaustion or missing permissions, Lambda deployment errors, and subnet sizing and IAM errors. Afterwards the reader can diagnose a failed deployment from its console state and logs.

articles.title: Resilience tooling on AWS: Resilience Hub vs Fault Injection Service vs Application Recovery Controller (zonal shift, zonal autoshift, Region switch)
articles.scope: Contrasts three jobs. Resilience Hub assesses resilience against RTO and RPO policies. FIS proves it with controlled faults and stop conditions, including AZ power-interruption scenarios. ARC acts on it during events with zonal shift, zonal autoshift and Region switch plans; routing controls are linked from cloud/aws/networking. Shows how to test Multi-AZ and multi-Region failover in CI and game days, and maps to Azure Chaos Studio and Azure's zonal resilience tooling. Afterwards the reader can design and evidence failover testing for a critical workload.

articles.title: Terraform on AWS: AWS and AWSCC providers, S3 backend with native state locking, OIDC from CI, multi-account provider aliases and CloudFormation interop
articles.scope: Holds only AWS-provider specifics; Terraform language, state and workflow concepts stay in devops/iac. Covers choosing the AWS vs AWSCC (Cloud Control) provider, the S3 backend with S3-native lock files instead of DynamoDB lock tables, and assume-role and OIDC authentication from GitHub Actions or CodeBuild. Also covers provider aliases for multi-account and multi-Region deployments, default tags, and coexisting with CloudFormation stacks and Control Tower. Afterwards the reader can run Terraform safely against an AWS organization.

articles.title: Artifact repositories on AWS: CodeArtifact for NuGet, PyPI and npm vs ECR vs S3, with upstreams, domains and cross-account access
articles.scope: Sets up a CodeArtifact domain and repositories with upstreams and external connections to nuget.org, PyPI and npm. Authenticates dotnet, pip and npm clients with short-lived tokens, shares packages across accounts with domain and repository policies, and decides when an artifact belongs in CodeArtifact, ECR or S3. Maps to Azure Artifacts and links software-supply-chain-on-aws for package origin controls. Afterwards the reader can publish and consume the library's .NET and Python packages privately.

articles.title: Hosting Angular on AWS: Amplify Hosting and Amplify Gen 2 vs S3 plus CloudFront, branch environments and previews
articles.scope: Deploys an Angular app two ways. The first is Amplify Hosting, with Git-connected branch deployments, pull-request previews, custom domains and SSR support. The second is an S3 bucket behind CloudFront with origin access control and cache invalidation in a pipeline; CloudFront depth is in cloud/aws/networking. Adds Amplify Gen 2 for code-first backends. Maps to Azure Static Web Apps (close). Afterwards the reader can choose and automate front-end hosting for dev, test and production branches.

articles.title: AWS cost visibility and allocation: Cost Explorer vs Data Exports vs S3 Storage Lens, tags, Cost Categories, split cost allocation data and Billing Conductor
articles.scope: Contrasts each visibility tool's purpose, granularity and latency. Explains CUR 2.0 and FOCUS 1.2 exports queried with Athena, with a legacy-name box because SAA-C03 and CLOUDOPS-A still say AWS Cost and Usage Report. Covers cost allocation tag activation, Cost Categories, split cost allocation data for ECS and EKS, S3 Storage Lens for storage spend, and Billing Conductor for pro forma showback; budgets and anomaly alerts are in estimating-and-guarding-aws-spend. Links architecture/cost for FinOps practice and maps to Microsoft Cost Management. Afterwards the reader can build showback for a multi-account organization.

articles.title: AWS purchasing models: On-Demand vs Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, Database, SageMaker AI) vs Reserved Instances vs Spot
articles.scope: Explains how commitments work, the order in which discounts apply, and the trade-off between flexibility and depth of discount. Covers the Database Savings Plans introduced in December 2025, Reserved Instance types and scope, Spot interruption handling, and coverage and utilization reporting, including how discounts apply to Lambda Managed Instances and ECS Managed Instances. Maps to Azure savings plans, reservations and Spot VMs. Afterwards the reader can recommend a commitment portfolio for a usage profile.

articles.title: Rightsizing and cost optimization on AWS: Compute Optimizer, Cost Optimization Hub, Trusted Advisor, storage tiering and data transfer costs
articles.scope: Uses Compute Optimizer, Cost Optimization Hub and Trusted Advisor checks to find idle and oversized resources and commitment opportunities. Explains data transfer pricing traps (inter-AZ, NAT gateway, cross-Region, internet egress, VPC endpoints) and storage tiering savings, linking cloud/aws/networking for the network constructs. Afterwards the reader can run a monthly optimization review and quantify the savings.

articles.title: Estimating and guarding AWS spend: Pricing Calculator, Free Tier plans, billing alarms vs Budgets vs Cost Anomaly Detection
articles.scope: Shows how to estimate a design with the Pricing Calculator, including in-console bill estimates that apply your discounts. Explains the credit-based Free Tier introduced in July 2025: either a Free plan with USD 100 at sign-up plus up to USD 100 earned, lasting up to six months, or a Paid plan, both alongside always-free allowances. Contrasts three guardrails: CloudWatch billing alarms, Budgets with budget actions, and Cost Anomaly Detection. Covers the cloud-economics basics CLF-C02 tests and ends with a safe-lab checklist for this library's exercises. Afterwards the reader can estimate a workload and cap the risk of surprise bills.

articles.title: AWS CDK in C# and Python: Constructs, Stages, cdk-nag, Tests and CDK Pipelines
articles.scope: Wave 2. Builds CDK v2 from the bottom up, with every example in both C# and Python. It covers the App > Stage > Stack > Construct tree and the three construct levels: L1 Cfn* resources, L2 intent-based constructs with grant methods and defaults, and L3 patterns. It shows escape hatches (AddPropertyOverride, node.defaultChild). It explains how CDK maps to CloudFormation: cdk synth writes templates and assets to cdk.out, and cdk deploy runs a change set. Further topics are bootstrapping (the CDKToolkit stack and its roles), context and environment-specific stacks, Aspects with cdk-nag (AwsSolutions pack, suppressions with reasons), fine-grained assertions and snapshot tests in xUnit and pytest, and CDK Pipelines (self-mutation, waves, stages, manual approvals). It also covers cdk diff, drift and cdk refactor. The article contrasts CDK with Bicep modules and Terraform and notes the CDKTF sunset (2025-12-10). It links to aws-cloudformation-in-depth, choosing-aws-iac-cloudformation-cdk-sam-terraform and compare/iac-devops/bicep-arm-vs-cloudformation-cdk.

articles.title: AWS Migration Services: Transform, Application Migration Service, DMS, Discovery, DataSync, Transfer Family and Snow
articles.scope: Wave 5. Explains which tool fits each phase of a migration. Assessment uses AWS Application Discovery Service (agentless collector or agent) and AWS Transform. Transform also replaces AWS Migration Hub, which stopped taking new customers on 2025-11-07; its strategy recommendations, journeys and orchestrator now live in Transform. Server rehost uses AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): replication agent, staging area, launch templates, test then cutover, post-launch actions. Databases use AWS DMS (instances vs DMS Serverless, full load plus CDC, homogeneous data migrations) and DMS Schema Conversion vs the legacy SCT desktop tool. Files use DataSync and Transfer Family (SFTP/FTPS/AS2). Offline transfer covers the Snow status: no new Snow Family customers, with DataSync, Data Transfer Terminal or Outposts as alternatives. It ends with how to secure migration tooling (SAP-C03 4.2.10) and a wave-planning walk-through. It mirrors azure-migrate-for-servers and moving-and-migrating-data-to-azure, and links to compare/resilience-migration/migration-azure-migrate-vs-aws-transform-and-mgn.

articles.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, Application Recovery Controller and Resilience Hub: Who Owns DR Orchestration
articles.scope: Wave 2. The AWS counterpart to azure-backup-vs-site-recovery. It covers Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS): continuous block-level replication from on-premises, other clouds or another Region, low-cost staging subnets, point-in-time recovery, drills without disruption, and failback. AWS-to-AWS coverage is EC2 only, so RDS and other managed services need their own replication. It covers Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC): routing controls with control panels and safety rules, zonal shift, zonal autoshift with practice runs, and Region switch plans for cross-account, multi-step Regional failover (added 2025-08). It covers Resilience Hub's resiliency policies, assessments and drift. The article sets out the split of responsibility across AWS Backup (data), DRS (servers), ARC (traffic and orchestration) and Resilience Hub (assurance), and maps each to the pilot light, warm standby and multi-site strategies. It links to aws-backup-and-data-resilience, resilience-tooling-on-aws and architecture/reliability/rto-rpo-dr-strategies.

articles.title: Centralized Security Logging on AWS: Organization Trail, Log Archive, Security Lake and Cross-Account Analysis
articles.scope: Wave 4. Builds a multi-account logging design step by step. It starts with an organization CloudTrail trail, set up from the management account or a delegated administrator, writing to a Control Tower-style log-archive account. Integrity comes from S3 Object Lock, SSE-KMS and log file validation. It then covers delegated administrators for GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie, Config, Inspector and Detective (SCS-C03 6.1.4). Security Lake adds OCSF normalisation, sources including third-party ones, and data-access vs query-access subscribers. CloudWatch cross-account observability uses OAM sinks and links, with Logs Insights and Athena queries and OpenSearch or Managed Grafana for correlation. Network log sources are VPC Flow Logs, Transit Gateway flow logs and Route 53 Resolver query logs. The article states that CloudTrail Lake has been closed to new customers since 2026-05-31 and that AWS points to CloudWatch instead. The Azure contrast covers a Log Analytics workspace design and the Sentinel data lake, linking to compare/security-services/sentinel-vs-security-lake-and-siem-on-aws.

articles.title: AWS Edge Security: WAF Rule Design, Bot Control, Shield Advanced and Firewall Manager
articles.scope: Wave 4. Turns the network-security-services-compared overview into working configuration. AWS WAF topics are web ACL capacity units, rule priority and labels, AWS managed rule groups (core rule set, known bad inputs, SQLi, IP reputation, anti-DDoS), Bot Control (common vs targeted), Fraud Control ATP and ACFP, rate-based rules with custom aggregation keys, geo match, CAPTCHA and challenge actions, and logging. Origin protection uses CloudFront OAC, VPC origins and custom-header checks, and the CloudFront flat-rate plans that bundle WAF. Shield Advanced covers protection groups, health-based detection, SRT and proactive engagement, automatic application-layer mitigation and cost protection. Firewall Manager applies WAF, Shield Advanced, security group, Network Firewall and DNS Firewall policies across an organization, and can use third-party rule groups from Marketplace. Examples are in CDK (C#) and Terraform. It mirrors Azure WAF on Front Door, DDoS Network Protection and Azure Firewall Manager, and links to security/network-security/edge-protection-waf-ddos.

articles.title: AWS AppConfig and feature flags in .NET and Python
articles.scope: Counterpart of azure-app-configuration-and-feature-flags. AppConfig applications, environments, configuration profiles, feature flags with variants, validators and deployment strategies with CloudWatch-alarm rollback; the AppConfig Agent for Lambda, ECS and EKS; Parameter Store as the plain key-value option; implemented in ASP.NET Core and Python with IAM roles.

terms.definition: A managed integration service that moves data between SaaS applications, such as Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow, and AWS services like S3 and Redshift on a schedule, on events or on demand, with mapping, filtering and validation.
terms.equivalent: azure: Logic Apps connectors / Data Factory SaaS connectors (partial)

terms.definition: A serverless interactive query service that runs Trino-based SQL, or Spark, directly over data in S3 using the AWS Glue Data Catalog, billed by data scanned.
terms.equivalent: azure: Synapse serverless SQL pool / Fabric SQL analytics endpoint (close)

terms.definition: A MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible database whose shared cluster volume keeps six copies across three AZs, supporting up to 15 low-lag replicas, Serverless v2 scaling and Global Database replication.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure HorizonDB (close; preview); Azure SQL Database Hyperscale (partial); Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server (partial)

terms.definition: A serverless, PostgreSQL-compatible distributed SQL database, separate from Aurora clusters, offering active-active multi-Region clusters with strong consistency and optimistic concurrency control.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: AWS's native observability service, covering metrics, logs, traces, alarms and dashboards along with application, container, database and network monitoring features.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Monitor (close)

terms.definition: A fully managed delivery service whose Firehose streams (formerly delivery streams) buffer streaming data, optionally transform it with Lambda and convert its format, then load it into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, Apache Iceberg tables or HTTP endpoints.
terms.equivalent: azure: Event Hubs Capture (partial) / Stream Analytics (partial)

terms.definition: An EBS feature that uses tag-based policies to automate the creation, retention, cross-Region copying and deletion of EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Backup disk backup policies (partial)

terms.definition: An investigation service that builds a behavior graph from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, EKS audit logs and GuardDuty findings to visualize the scope and root cause of security incidents.
terms.equivalent: azure: Microsoft Sentinel investigation graph / Defender XDR incidents (partial)

terms.definition: A MongoDB API-compatible document database that separates storage from compute in the Aurora style, offered as instance-based or elastic clusters.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (close)

terms.definition: A serverless key-value and document NoSQL database that delivers single-digit-millisecond performance at any scale, with on-demand or provisioned capacity, transactions, TTL and point-in-time recovery.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL (close)

terms.definition: AWS's managed OCI registry, comprising private repositories and the ECR Public gallery, with IAM repository policies, lifecycle rules, vulnerability scanning, replication, pull-through cache and managed image signing.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Container Registry (close)

terms.definition: AWS's fully managed container orchestrator, which runs tasks and long-running services from task definitions on Fargate, EC2 or ECS Managed Instances capacity.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Container Apps (partial)

terms.definition: A serverless, elastic NFSv4 file system that thousands of Linux clients across AZs can mount at once, with Elastic, Provisioned or Bursting throughput and lifecycle-managed storage classes.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Files NFS shares (close)

terms.definition: AWS's managed Kubernetes service, which runs a conformant, highly available control plane and integrates clusters with IAM, VPC networking, load balancing and storage.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Kubernetes Service (close)

terms.definition: Managed in-memory caching on the Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached engines, in serverless or node-based clusters, with replication, cluster-mode sharding and cross-Region Global Datastore.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Managed Redis / Azure Cache for Redis (close)

terms.definition: A managed big-data platform that runs Apache Spark, Hive, Trino, HBase and other frameworks on EC2 clusters, on EKS or as EMR Serverless.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Databricks / Fabric Spark / HDInsight (partial)

terms.definition: A serverless event router whose buses match events from AWS services, SaaS partners and your applications against rule patterns and deliver them, optionally transformed, to targets. It also offers a schema registry, archive and replay, Pipes and Scheduler.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Event Grid (close)

terms.definition: A family of managed third-party file systems: FSx for Windows File Server (SMB with Active Directory), FSx for Lustre (HPC and ML), FSx for NetApp ONTAP (multiprotocol, with snapshots and tiering) and FSx for OpenZFS.
