terms.definition: A CloudWatch setup that links source accounts, one by one or through Organizations, to a monitoring account that can view, query and alarm on their metrics, logs and traces.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Monitor cross-subscription and cross-workspace queries (partial)

terms.definition: CloudWatch's database observability experience for RDS and Aurora, in Standard and Advanced modes, showing DB load, top SQL and wait events; it supersedes the Performance Insights console, a name CLOUDOPS-A skill 1.3.5 still uses.
terms.equivalent: azure: Query Performance Insight / database watcher (partial)

terms.definition: A structured JSON log format from which CloudWatch Logs extracts metrics automatically, so code can emit custom metrics asynchronously through log output instead of API calls.
terms.equivalent: azure: Application Insights custom metrics (partial)

terms.definition: A generative-AI CloudWatch feature that starts from an alarm, a metric or a Logs Insights query, correlates telemetry, deployment events and CloudTrail change events into hypotheses, and can suggest Systems Manager Automation runbooks.
terms.equivalent: azure: Copilot in Azure observability investigations (partial)

terms.definition: A CloudWatch feature, delivered as a Lambda extension, that records system-level function metrics such as memory, CPU, network use and cold starts.
terms.equivalent: azure: Application Insights for Azure Functions (partial)

terms.definition: Log ingestion and storage organized into log groups and streams, with per-group retention, Standard and Infrequent Access classes, KMS encryption, data protection masking and anomaly detection.
terms.equivalent: azure: Log Analytics workspace (close)

terms.definition: Log-group data protection policies that use managed or custom data identifiers to detect sensitive data such as credentials and PII and mask it, with unmasking controlled by the logs:Unmask permission.
terms.equivalent: azure: Log Analytics workspace transformations that drop or hash fields (partial)

terms.definition: An interactive query engine over CloudWatch Logs for filtering, parsing, aggregating and visualizing log data, in its own query language, OpenSearch PPL or SQL.
terms.equivalent: azure: Log Analytics KQL queries (close)

terms.definition: A time series identified by namespace, name and dimensions at standard (60-second) or high (1-second) resolution, offered as OpenTelemetry metrics queried with PromQL (recommended) or as Classic metrics.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Monitor platform and custom metrics (close)

terms.definition: A pattern on a log group that turns matching log events into CloudWatch metric values for alarms and dashboards; it applies only to events ingested after it is created.
terms.equivalent: azure: log search alert rules (partial)

terms.definition: A CloudWatch feature that streams selected metrics continuously, in JSON or OpenTelemetry format, through Data Firehose to S3 or partner observability platforms with minimal latency.
terms.equivalent: azure: diagnostic settings metric export to Event Hubs (partial)

terms.definition: CloudWatch's three network observability tools: Internet Monitor for internet-to-application performance, Network Flow Monitor for agent-measured flow loss and latency, and Network Synthetic Monitor for probes to on-premises over Direct Connect.
terms.equivalent: azure: Network Watcher Connection Monitor (close)

terms.definition: An AI-powered, OpenTelemetry-based CloudWatch experience for applications and AI agents. It discovers services from telemetry, writes SQL or PromQL from plain-language questions, scores agent responses with evaluators, and is also available as an IDE extension.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Monitor Application Insights agent observability (partial)

terms.definition: Real user monitoring that collects page-load, JavaScript error and HTTP performance data from real browser sessions through a web client snippet; it suits an Angular front end.
terms.equivalent: azure: Application Insights JavaScript SDK (close)

terms.definition: A log-group setting that streams matching log events in near real time to Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, Data Firehose or OpenSearch, including destinations in other accounts.
terms.equivalent: azure: diagnostic settings streaming to Event Hubs (partial)

terms.definition: Scheduled canary scripts, in Node.js or Python, that probe endpoints, APIs and user flows from AWS and publish availability and latency metrics, screenshots and HAR files.
terms.equivalent: azure: Application Insights availability tests (close)

terms.definition: The rule that controls how fast CodeDeploy shifts traffic or updates instances, such as AllAtOnce, HalfAtATime or OneAtATime with a minimum healthy hosts value for EC2, or Canary10Percent5Minutes or Linear10PercentEvery1Minute for Lambda and ECS.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Pipelines rolling and canary deployment strategies (partial)

terms.definition: Machine-to-machine authorization in a Cognito user pool, in which confidential app clients use the OAuth 2.0 client-credentials grant to obtain access tokens scoped to the custom scopes of resource servers.
terms.equivalent: azure: Microsoft Entra ID app registrations with client credentials and app roles (close)

terms.definition: The AWS Continuum frontier agent, formerly AWS Security Agent, that learns application context from design documents, user stories and IaC, runs on-demand penetration tests of deployed applications and source code, and returns validated, reproducible findings with fixes.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: An in-memory, write-through cache cluster for DynamoDB that serves eventually consistent reads in microseconds through a DynamoDB-compatible API.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB integrated cache (close)

terms.definition: DynamoDB's two billing models: on-demand bills per read and write request and scales automatically, while provisioned bills for configured read and write capacity units, with optional auto scaling and reserved capacity.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB serverless vs provisioned or autoscale RU/s (close)

terms.definition: IAM policy conditions, such as dynamodb:LeadingKeys and dynamodb:Attributes, that restrict a principal to items whose partition key matches its identity and to selected attributes.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: A DynamoDB index with its own partition key and optional sort key and separate throughput, offering only eventually consistent reads, that can be added or removed at any time.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB global secondary index (close)

terms.definition: Multi-Region, multi-active table replicas that use either multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC, last writer wins; can span accounts) or multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC).
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB multi-region writes (close)

terms.definition: A DynamoDB index that shares the table's partition key but uses an alternate sort key; it must be defined when the table is created, supports strongly consistent reads and caps each item collection at 10 GB.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB composite index within a logical partition (partial)

terms.definition: DynamoDB's primary key: a partition key that is hashed to place items on partitions, optionally combined with a sort key that orders items within an item collection and enables range queries.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB partition key plus id (partial)

terms.definition: Continuous backups that restore a table, as a new table, to any second within a configurable recovery period of up to 35 days.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB continuous backup (close)

terms.definition: A 24-hour change log of table modifications, ordered per item, that Lambda or KCL consumers read for triggers, replication, auditing and event-driven designs.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB change feed (close)

terms.definition: Per-table storage classes, Standard and Standard-Infrequent Access; Standard-IA lowers the storage price for rarely read data in exchange for higher read and write request prices.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: All-or-nothing TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems operations over up to 100 items in one or more tables in a Region, costing twice the capacity of standard operations.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB transactional batch within a logical partition (partial)

terms.definition: A per-item expiry-timestamp attribute after which DynamoDB deletes the item in the background without consuming write capacity, recording the deletion in DynamoDB Streams.
terms.equivalent: azure: Cosmos DB time to live (close)

terms.definition: An ECS capability that registers on-premises or other-cloud servers as external instances through an SSM activation, so the Region's ECS control plane can schedule tasks on them.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes (partial)

terms.definition: An ECS object that tells the scheduler where to place tasks (Fargate, Fargate Spot, an Auto Scaling group or ECS Managed Instances) and can scale that capacity through managed scaling.
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS node pools / Container Apps workload profiles (partial)

terms.definition: An ECS rolling-update setting that stops a deployment whose tasks repeatedly fail to start or to pass health checks and, if rollback is enabled, returns the service to its last completed deployment.
terms.equivalent: azure: Container Apps revision health probes and activation (partial)

terms.definition: An ECS feature that opens an interactive shell, or runs a single command, inside a running container over the Systems Manager Session Manager channel, with IAM control and session logging and no SSH or open ports.
terms.equivalent: azure: az containerapp exec (close)

terms.definition: An ECS feature that builds a Fargate web service with a URL, HTTPS on an Application Load Balancer shared across Express services, auto scaling and monitoring, from a container image, a task execution role and an infrastructure role; it is AWS's recommended path off App Runner.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Container Apps (partial: no scale to zero, KEDA or Dapr)

terms.definition: An ECS compute option in which AWS provisions, patches, drains and scales EC2 instances in your account for your tasks, while you keep the choice of instance type and EC2 pricing.
terms.equivalent: azure: Container Apps dedicated workload profiles (partial)

terms.term: ECS built-in blue/green, linear and canary deployments
terms.definition: ECS deployment strategies, added in 2025, that shift load balancer or Service Connect traffic between service revisions all at once, linearly or as a canary, with lifecycle hooks, test listeners and bake time and without CodeDeploy.
terms.equivalent: azure: Container Apps revisions with traffic splitting (close)

terms.definition: ECS-managed service-to-service networking that adds a proxy to each task to provide Cloud Map-based discovery, load balancing, retries and traffic metrics within a namespace; it is the documented migration path from App Mesh for ECS workloads.
terms.equivalent: azure: Container Apps built-in service discovery or Dapr service invocation (partial)

terms.definition: The versioned JSON blueprint for an ECS task that declares its container images, CPU and memory, ports, health checks, logging, secrets, volumes, network mode, task role and task execution role.
terms.equivalent: azure: Container Apps container template (close)

terms.definition: The IAM role that the ECS agent and Fargate use on your behalf to pull images from ECR, send logs and fetch referenced secrets before and while containers start.
terms.equivalent: azure: managed identity used for ACR pull and Key Vault references (partial)

terms.definition: The IAM role whose temporary credentials are delivered to application code inside an ECS task, which uses them to call AWS APIs.
terms.equivalent: azure: managed identity assigned to a container app (close)

terms.definition: EKS API objects that grant IAM principals access to a cluster's Kubernetes API, optionally through AWS-managed access policies; they replace the aws-auth ConfigMap.
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS with Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes (close)

terms.definition: Software for creating and running Kubernetes clusters on your own infrastructure (vSphere, bare metal, Nutanix and others) using EKS Distro, with optional paid AWS support but no AWS-managed control plane.
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS on Azure Local (partial)

terms.definition: An EKS operating mode in which AWS manages Karpenter-based node provisioning and scaling, OS patching and core add-ons such as pod networking, block storage and load balancing.
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS Automatic (close)

terms.definition: AWS-managed platform features attached to a cluster that run open-source tools for you, currently Argo CD for GitOps, AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) and Kube Resource Orchestrator (kro).
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS GitOps with the Flux extension (partial)

terms.definition: The open-source Kubernetes distribution, with the versions and patches that Amazon EKS runs, which you can deploy and operate yourself anywhere.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: An EKS feature that joins on-premises or edge servers as worker nodes to a cluster whose control plane runs in an AWS Region, over private connectivity, using SSM or IAM Roles Anywhere for node credentials.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes (partial)

terms.definition: An EKS feature that associates a Kubernetes service account with an IAM role through an EKS API and a node agent, delivering temporary credentials to pods without a per-cluster OIDC provider.
terms.equivalent: azure: Microsoft Entra Workload ID for AKS (partial: same outcome, but Workload ID federates over OIDC like IRSA)

terms.definition: EventBridge features that store events matching a pattern in an archive for a set retention period and later replay them onto a bus, to recover from failures or test new rules.
terms.equivalent: azure: none in Event Grid; Event Hubs retention and replay (partial)

terms.definition: Point-to-point integrations that read from a source such as SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams or MSK, optionally filter and enrich the events, and deliver them to a single target without glue code.
terms.equivalent: azure: Logic Apps workflow with built-in connectors (partial)

terms.definition: A serverless scheduler for one-time, rate and cron schedules with time zones and flexible time windows that invokes AWS service APIs directly; it is separate from the older scheduled rules on an event bus.
terms.equivalent: azure: Logic Apps recurrence trigger / Functions timer trigger (partial)

terms.definition: An ECS-only Fargate capacity provider that runs interruptible tasks on spare capacity at a discount, giving a two-minute warning (a task state change event and SIGTERM) before reclaiming them.
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS Spot node pools (partial)

terms.definition: The original EKS pattern in which pods exchange a projected service-account OIDC token for IAM role credentials by calling sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity against the cluster's OIDC provider.
terms.equivalent: azure: Microsoft Entra Workload ID federated identity credentials (close)

terms.definition: AWS's agentic AI IDE and CLI, which turns specifications into designs, tasks and code, with agent hooks and MCP support; AWS recommends it for its latest AI coding capabilities.
terms.equivalent: azure: GitHub Copilot agent mode in VS Code (partial)

terms.definition: A KMS key store backed by your own AWS CloudHSM cluster or by an external key manager outside AWS, used when regulation requires control over the key material.
terms.equivalent: azure: Managed HSM / HSM-backed keys (partial)

terms.definition: Non-secret key-value pairs bound to a KMS encryption as additional authenticated data; they must match exactly on decrypt, appear in CloudTrail and can be required by policy conditions.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: A key-specific permission, created programmatically, that lets a grantee principal use a KMS key for listed operations, optionally limited by encryption context, without editing the key policy; AWS services use grants for features such as EBS encryption.
terms.equivalent: azure: none, because Key Vault uses RBAC role assignments (none)

terms.definition: The mandatory resource policy on every KMS key that defines who can administer and use it; IAM identity policies take effect only if the key policy delegates to the account, whereas grants are a separate delegation mechanism.
terms.equivalent: azure: Key Vault RBAC role assignments on keys (partial)

terms.definition: The three ownership types for KMS keys (formerly called customer master keys): customer managed keys you control, AWS managed keys created per service under aws/ aliases and rotated yearly, and AWS owned keys used invisibly across accounts.
terms.equivalent: azure: customer-managed vs Microsoft-managed keys (close)

terms.definition: A set of interoperable KMS keys in different Regions that share a key ID and key material, so data encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in another without re-encryption.
terms.equivalent: azure: Key Vault key backup and restore within a geography (partial)

terms.definition: An API Gateway authorizer that runs your Lambda function to validate a bearer token or request parameters and returns an IAM policy (REST APIs) or a simple allow response (HTTP APIs), with optional caching of the result.
terms.equivalent: azure: API Management validate-jwt and send-request policies (partial)

terms.definition: Targets (SQS, SNS, Lambda, EventBridge, or S3 for failures) that receive an invocation record holding the result or error of an asynchronous invocation or a failed event-source-mapping batch.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: A capability of Event Functions that uses checkpoint and replay through the Durable Execution SDK (including .NET and Python) to run multi-step workflows for up to one year, suspending during waits without compute charges.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Durable Functions (close)

terms.definition: The original Lambda function type under its new name: a handler in a managed or custom runtime that runs in response to events or invocations for up to 15 minutes; APIs, SDKs, ARNs and AWS::Lambda::Function still say function.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Functions (close)

terms.definition: A Lambda-managed poller that reads batches from SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, MSK, Amazon MQ or DocumentDB and invokes a function, with batching windows, filtering and reporting of partial batch failures.
terms.equivalent: azure: Functions Service Bus and Event Hubs triggers (close)

terms.definition: Companion processes, internal or external, that run in the execution environment to integrate monitoring, security or secret-caching tools through the Extensions and Telemetry APIs; they are usually delivered as layers.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: A dedicated HTTPS endpoint for an Event Function with AWS_IAM or NONE auth, CORS and response streaming, but no usage plans, caching or WAF of its own.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Functions HTTP trigger endpoint (close)

terms.definition: The three ways an Event Function is invoked: synchronous (the caller waits and handles errors), asynchronous (Lambda queues the event and retries twice) and event source mapping (Lambda polls a stream or queue and invokes in batches).
terms.equivalent: azure: Functions triggers and bindings (partial)

terms.definition: Versioned .zip archives of libraries, custom runtimes or configuration that are extracted into /opt and shared across functions, up to five per function; container-image functions do not use them.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: A Lambda compute type that runs Event Functions on Lambda-managed EC2 instances in your account through capacity providers. It has multi-concurrent execution environments, CPU-based scaling without cold starts (three instances by default) and EC2 pricing plus a 15% management fee; Savings Plans and RIs discount only the EC2 portion.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Functions on an App Service plan (partial)

terms.definition: A Lambda compute primitive that launches VM-isolated environments from snapshots of customer-built MicroVM images, each with its own HTTPS endpoint and with suspend and resume that preserves memory and disk, for a total lifespan of up to 8 hours.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions (close)

terms.definition: Pre-initialized execution environments kept ready for a published version or alias to remove cold-start latency, billed for as long as they are configured.
terms.equivalent: azure: Functions Premium or Flex Consumption always-ready instances (close)

terms.definition: A free per-function setting that both guarantees and caps how many concurrent executions the function can take from the account's Regional concurrency quota.
terms.equivalent: azure: Functions maximum instance count (partial)

terms.definition: A feature that snapshots the initialized execution environment of a published version and resumes new environments from that snapshot, cutting cold starts for Java, Python 3.12+ and .NET 8+; caching and restore are charged for Python and .NET.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: Versions are immutable, numbered snapshots of a function's code and configuration; aliases are named pointers to one version, or two with weighted routing. Together they give stable ARNs, canary traffic shifting and instant rollback.
terms.equivalent: azure: Functions deployment slots (partial)

terms.definition: A Lambda compute primitive that runs a Node.js HTTP server (Express, Hono, React Router), deployed as a .zip, behind a Lambda-provided HTTPS endpoint. Execution environments serve many requests at once, endpoints route to immutable revisions, and the service scales to zero and can route by latency across Regions.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Container Apps HTTP apps with scale to zero (partial); Azure Functions Flex Consumption (partial)

terms.definition: An open-source file client that mounts a bucket as a local file system for high-throughput reads and sequential writes of new objects, but without full POSIX semantics such as renames or in-place edits.
terms.equivalent: azure: BlobFuse2 (close)

terms.definition: An open-source developer toolkit for Lambda in Python, TypeScript, Java and .NET that provides structured logging, EMF metrics, tracing, idempotency, batch processing, parameter retrieval and data masking.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: An RDS and Aurora feature that keeps a synchronized staging copy of a production database for upgrades or schema changes and switches over, typically with under a minute of downtime.
terms.equivalent: azure: none first-party (none)

terms.definition: Sign-in to RDS and Aurora MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL with short-lived (15-minute) tokens generated from IAM credentials, instead of stored database passwords.
terms.equivalent: azure: Microsoft Entra authentication for Azure SQL and flexible server (close)

terms.definition: A high-availability configuration with automatic failover behind the same endpoint: either one synchronous standby (Multi-AZ DB instance) or two readable standbys (Multi-AZ DB cluster) in other AZs.
terms.equivalent: azure: zone-redundant high availability in flexible server (close)

terms.definition: A managed connection pooler for RDS and Aurora that multiplexes application connections, shortens the impact of failover and supports IAM and Secrets Manager authentication.
terms.equivalent: azure: built-in PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server (partial)

terms.definition: An asynchronously replicated, readable copy of an RDS database, in the same or another Region, that scales reads and can be promoted to a standalone database for disaster recovery.
terms.equivalent: azure: flexible server read replicas / Azure SQL geo-replicas (close)

terms.definition: An RDS setting that raises allocated storage automatically, without downtime, when free space runs low, up to a configured maximum.
terms.equivalent: azure: flexible server storage autogrow (close)

terms.term: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
terms.definition: A managed OpenShift service operated jointly by Red Hat and AWS, with a hosted control plane option and billing through AWS.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Red Hat OpenShift (exact)

terms.definition: Named endpoints attached to a bucket, each with its own access policy and an optional VPC-only restriction, that simplify access to shared datasets; Multi-Region Access Points add one global endpoint routing to replicated buckets in several Regions.
terms.equivalent: azure: private endpoints plus container-scoped RBAC (partial)

terms.definition: A managed job runner that applies one operation, such as copying, tagging, restoring, invoking Lambda, setting Object Lock retention or replicating existing objects, to billions of objects listed in an inventory or manifest, with completion reports.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob batch API / AzCopy jobs (partial)

terms.definition: Account- and bucket-level settings, on by default for new buckets, that override any ACL or bucket policy granting public access; they are the first control to check when a bucket is unexpectedly public.
terms.equivalent: azure: storage account setting that disallows anonymous blob access (close)

terms.definition: Bucket configurations that send object-level events, such as ObjectCreated or ObjectRemoved, directly to SNS, SQS or Lambda, or to EventBridge for richer filtering and more targets.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob Storage events through Event Grid (close)

terms.definition: A single-AZ, high-performance storage class held in directory buckets with session-based authorization, offering single-digit-millisecond access for latency-sensitive workloads such as ML training and analytics.
terms.equivalent: azure: premium block blob storage (partial)

terms.definition: An S3 storage class that moves each object between frequent, infrequent and archive instant access tiers, and optional archive tiers, according to access, for a small per-object monitoring fee and no retrieval charges.
terms.equivalent: azure: lifecycle management with last-access-time tracking (partial)

terms.definition: Bucket rules that, after set ages, transition objects between storage classes and expire current versions, noncurrent versions, delete markers and incomplete multipart uploads.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob lifecycle management policy (close)

terms.definition: An upload pattern that sends an object as independently retried parts in parallel and then assembles them; it is recommended for large objects and required above the 5 GB single-PUT limit.
terms.equivalent: azure: block blobs staged with Put Block and Put Block List (exact)

terms.definition: Write-once-read-many protection that stops object versions being deleted or overwritten, for a retention period in governance or compliance mode or indefinitely under a legal hold.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob immutable storage with time-based retention and legal hold (close)

terms.definition: A bucket setting that controls ACLs; its default mode, bucket owner enforced, disables ACLs so the bucket owner owns every object and only policies govern access.
terms.equivalent: azure: none needed, because Azure Storage has no object ACLs (none)

terms.definition: A time-limited URL, or presigned POST, signed with the creator's credentials that lets whoever holds it GET or PUT one specific object without AWS credentials of their own.
terms.equivalent: azure: shared access signature (SAS) (close)

terms.definition: Asynchronous, rule-based copying of objects between buckets in different Regions (CRR) or the same Region (SRR), with an optional 15-minute Replication Time Control SLA and Batch Replication for existing objects.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob object replication (close) / geo-redundant storage (partial)

terms.definition: A bucket setting that charges the requester, not the bucket owner, for requests and downloaded data, and therefore requires authenticated requests.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: S3's at-rest encryption modes: SSE-S3 (the default), SSE-KMS (cheaper with S3 Bucket Keys), DSSE-KMS (dual-layer) and SSE-C (keys supplied per request), which since April 2026 is blocked by default on new general purpose buckets.
terms.equivalent: azure: Storage service encryption with Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys (close)

terms.definition: Per-object tiers that trade availability, AZ resilience, latency, minimum duration, minimum billable size and retrieval fees against storage price: Standard, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, Express One Zone, and Glacier Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob access tiers Hot, Cool, Cold and Archive (close)

terms.definition: Organization-wide analytics for S3 usage, activity and data-protection posture, with free and advanced metrics, dashboards and recommendations.
terms.equivalent: azure: Storage insights in Azure Monitor (partial)

terms.definition: S3 table buckets that store tabular data as Apache Iceberg tables with built-in compaction and snapshot management, integrated with AWS analytics engines through the Glue Data Catalog.
terms.equivalent: azure: OneLake Delta tables in Microsoft Fabric (partial)

terms.definition: A bucket feature that routes uploads and downloads through CloudFront edge locations and over the AWS backbone to speed up long-distance transfers, for an extra per-GB fee.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: S3 vector buckets and vector indexes that store and query embeddings with low-cost, sub-second similarity search, used directly or as storage behind Bedrock Knowledge Bases and OpenSearch.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure AI Search vector indexes (partial)

terms.definition: A bucket setting that keeps every version of every object and turns deletes into delete markers, optionally protected by MFA Delete, so overwritten or deleted data can be restored.
terms.equivalent: azure: Blob versioning (close)

terms.definition: Billing data, delivered in CUR 2.0, that allocates the cost of shared EC2 instances to individual ECS tasks and EKS pods according to the CPU and memory they reserve or use.
terms.equivalent: azure: AKS cost analysis add-on (close)

terms.definition: A queue that receives messages from a source queue once they exceed maxReceiveCount, and from which they can be redriven back to the source after the defect is fixed.
terms.equivalent: azure: Service Bus dead-letter subqueue (close)

terms.definition: Java and Python client libraries that store SQS or SNS payloads larger than the 1 MiB message limit in S3 and send a pointer instead, implementing the claim-check pattern.
terms.equivalent: azure: Service Bus Premium large-message support (partial)

terms.definition: A standard-queue feature that uses message group IDs to identify tenants and stops one noisy tenant's backlog from raising dwell time for the others, without FIFO's ordering limits.
terms.equivalent: azure: none (none)

terms.definition: An SQS queue type that keeps strict order within each MessageGroupId and deduplicates sends by MessageDeduplicationId or content hash within a five-minute window, with an optional high-throughput mode.
terms.equivalent: azure: Service Bus sessions with duplicate detection (close)

terms.definition: Receiving SQS messages with a wait time of up to 20 seconds, so the call returns as soon as a message arrives; compared with short polling, this cuts empty responses and request cost.
terms.equivalent: azure: Service Bus receive with a server wait time (close)

terms.definition: The period (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours) after a consumer receives an SQS message during which the message is hidden from other consumers; if it is not deleted in time, it becomes visible again.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Queue Storage visibility timeout (exact); Service Bus peek-lock duration (close)

terms.definition: A Systems Manager document that defines multi-step automated actions (API calls, scripts, approvals, branching), run on demand, on a schedule, from EventBridge or as AWS Config remediation.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Automation runbook (close)

terms.definition: An activation code and ID, bound to an IAM service role, that registers on-premises or other-cloud servers as Systems Manager managed nodes with mi- identifiers.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Arc-enabled servers onboarding (close)

terms.definition: A Systems Manager capability that collects metadata from managed nodes, such as installed applications, files, network configuration and Windows updates, and can sync it to S3 through Resource Data Sync for Athena queries.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Machine Configuration inventory / Change Tracking and Inventory (close)

terms.definition: Systems Manager schedules that define when potentially disruptive tasks (Run Command, Automation, Lambda or Step Functions) run against registered targets.
terms.equivalent: azure: Maintenance Configurations (close)

terms.definition: A central place to view, investigate and resolve operational work items (OpsItems) created from EventBridge rules, CloudWatch alarms, Config or Security Hub, with associated runbooks; it is the remaining option now that Incident Manager is closed to new customers.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Monitor alerts with ITSM integration (partial)

terms.definition: Hierarchical storage for configuration and secrets as String, StringList or KMS-encrypted SecureString parameters, in Standard or Advanced tiers, with no built-in rotation.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure App Configuration (close)

terms.definition: A Systems Manager capability that automates OS and application patching of managed nodes with patch baselines and patch policies or patch groups, scanning or installing in maintenance windows and reporting compliance.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Update Manager (close)

terms.definition: A Systems Manager capability that runs an SSM Command document, such as AWS-RunShellScript or AWS-RunPowerShellScript, on demand across targeted managed nodes, with rate and error controls and output to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
terms.equivalent: azure: VM Run Command (close)

terms.definition: A Systems Manager capability that opens audited shell or port-forwarding sessions to managed nodes through SSM Agent, with no inbound ports, bastion hosts or SSH keys.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Bastion (partial)

terms.definition: A Systems Manager capability that keeps managed nodes in a defined state by associating SSM documents with targets on a schedule and reapplying them to correct drift.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Machine Configuration (close)

terms.definition: A Map state mode that runs up to 10,000 parallel child workflow executions over items such as S3 objects or CSV rows, for large-scale batch processing.

pairs.difference: Application code uses the task role to call AWS APIs. The ECS agent uses the execution role to pull images, write logs and fetch secrets before the code runs.

Pod Identity uses an EKS association API and a node agent, so it needs no per-cluster OIDC provider and has simpler role trust. IRSA needs an IAM OIDC provider and a web-identity trust policy for each cluster.

Both give pods cloud credentials without secrets. Workload ID federates a projected service-account token over OIDC, which is IRSA's mechanism, whereas Pod Identity relies on an AWS node agent and association API.

Both exchange a projected Kubernetes service-account token through OIDC federation. Workload ID binds it to an Entra app or managed identity through federated identity credentials rather than an IAM role trust policy.
ECS is an AWS-proprietary orchestrator with no control-plane fee and a smaller API. EKS runs upstream Kubernetes for portability and ecosystem tooling, at the cost of more to operate.
Fargate hides instances entirely and bills by task size. ECS Managed Instances runs AWS-managed EC2 instances in your account, so you choose instance types, including GPUs, and can use EC2 pricing.
App Runner, closed to new customers from 2026-04-30, could build from source. Express Mode needs a container image but creates an ordinary ECS service, ALB and scaling that you can customize later.

Container Apps is a dedicated serverless container platform with scale to zero, KEDA event scaling, Dapr and revision traffic splitting. Express Mode scaffolds standard Fargate, ALB and auto scaling resources that stay visible in your account, and has none of those features.

An Event Function is a handler invoked once per event in a managed runtime in any supported language. A Web Function is a Node.js HTTP server on a Lambda HTTPS endpoint that serves many concurrent requests per environment and scales to zero.

Both host HTTP apps without servers to manage. Web Functions scale to zero and bill active CPU, but support Node.js only. Express Mode runs any container image on Fargate behind an ALB, with no scale to zero.

Both give each user or job an isolated, fast-starting sandbox for untrusted code. MicroVMs are built from your Dockerfile snapshot, can suspend and resume with memory and disk preserved, and live up to 8 hours; dynamic sessions are allocated from pre-warmed pools and are discarded after a cooldown.

AgentCore Code Interpreter is a managed code-execution tool for agents, with a fixed environment. MicroVMs are a general-purpose isolated compute primitive in which you control the image, ports and lifecycle.
Reserved concurrency is a free cap and guarantee on concurrent executions. Provisioned concurrency pays for pre-initialized environments that remove cold starts.

SnapStart resumes new environments from a cached snapshot of initialized state, so cold starts are shorter but still occur. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm, so there is no cold start, and charges for every configured hour.
A function URL is a free, single-function endpoint with IAM or no auth. An HTTP API adds routing across many backends, JWT authorizers, custom domains and throttling, for a per-request price.
Destinations receive a full invocation record (payload, error and context) for successful or failed asynchronous invocations. A DLQ holds only the original failed message once retries are exhausted.

Durable functions express a workflow as ordinary C# or Python code, checkpointed inside Lambda. Step Functions is a separate service with a JSON or visual state machine and native integrations with more than 220 services.
REST APIs add usage plans, caching, request validation, WAF and private endpoints. HTTP APIs are cheaper and faster, with native JWT authorizers, but lack those features.
Web PubSub is a hub with groups and broadcast built in. API Gateway WebSocket APIs route messages to backends, which must track connection IDs and loop over @connections to fan out.

AppSync Events and Web PubSub both provide serverless WebSocket channels with broadcast to subscribers. AppSync Events uses channel namespaces with event handlers and AWS auth modes, while Web PubSub uses hubs, groups and Entra or connection-string auth.
SQS stores each message until one consumer polls and deletes it. SNS pushes every message immediately to all subscribers and stores nothing, which is why the two are combined for durable fan-out.

SNS is high-throughput fan-out with attribute or payload filters. EventBridge adds content-based routing on any event field, a schema registry, archive and replay, and SaaS and AWS service events, but has lower throughput per target.

FIFO queues use message group IDs to enforce strict ordering, at the cost of throughput limits. Fair queues use the same IDs only to stop one tenant's backlog from delaying the others in a standard queue, without ordering.
Both hide a received message for a configurable period and make it visible again unless the consumer deletes it; only the limits and API names differ.

Service Bus is a broker with built-in sessions, transactions, scheduled delivery and peek-lock. SQS is a simpler queue with near-unlimited scale, where FIFO groups and DLQs approximate some of those features.

Scheduled rules are cron or rate rules on an event bus with limited targets and UTC only. Scheduler is a separate service that supports one-time schedules, time zones, flexible windows and millions of schedules that call APIs directly.
Both route events to handlers by filters. EventBridge adds archive and replay, a schema registry, Pipes and Scheduler, while Event Grid adds an MQTT broker and CloudEvents-native namespaces.
Kinesis Data Streams is a replayable stream that you consume with your own code. Firehose is a managed loader that buffers data and delivers it to destinations, with no consumers and no replay.

Kinesis is an AWS-native stream whose capacity is managed in shards and which integrates simply with IAM. MSK runs real Apache Kafka, with Kafka APIs, consumer groups, connectors and log compaction, but you manage brokers or Serverless quotas.
Event Hubs speaks the Kafka protocol on a proprietary engine without brokers to manage. MSK runs actual Kafka clusters, with full broker configuration, Kafka Connect and compacted topics.
Both are managed workflow engines. Step Functions focuses on orchestrating AWS services with Standard and Express semantics, while Logic Apps leans on a large catalogue of SaaS connectors.

Both orchestrate code by replay. Azure Durable Functions has orchestrator, activity and entity function types on a storage backend, while Lambda durable functions wraps one handler whose steps and waits Lambda manages.

Service Connect is ECS-only, sidecar-based service discovery and traffic management within a namespace. VPC Lattice is a managed application-networking service across VPCs and accounts for ECS, EKS, Lambda and EC2, with IAM auth policies.
Both are jointly operated, managed OpenShift offerings. Differences are limited to the cloud integrations (IAM vs Entra ID), billing and support routing.
ElastiCache is a cache whose data can be lost on failure. MemoryDB writes every change to a Multi-AZ transaction log, so it can be the system of record, at the cost of higher write latency.
Versioning lets you recover old versions, but anyone with permission can still delete them. Object Lock makes versions immutable for a retention period, and compliance mode blocks even the root user.

Native notifications go to SNS, SQS or Lambda, with only prefix and suffix filters. Turning on the EventBridge integration sends every bucket event to the bus for content filtering, archive and replay, and many targets.

EFS is a native NFS file system whose data lives only in EFS. S3 Files keeps the authoritative data in S3, caches the active working set on EFS-based storage and synchronizes both ways, so the same data stays reachable through S3 APIs.

Mountpoint is a free client-side FUSE mount optimized for large sequential reads and writes of new objects, without full POSIX semantics. S3 Files is a managed NFS file system with locking, POSIX permissions and two-way synchronization, billed for cache storage and access.

S3 Vectors is low-cost, durable vector storage with sub-second similarity queries and no cluster. The OpenSearch vector engine adds low-latency hybrid search, filtering and aggregations on provisioned or serverless compute, and can offload cold vectors to S3 Vectors.

DLM automates EBS snapshots and AMIs only, through tag-based policies at no extra charge. AWS Backup centralizes policy-driven backups across many services and accounts, with vaults, Vault Lock, restore testing and audit reports.

Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers' block storage, giving RPOs of seconds and recovery instances within minutes. AWS Backup takes scheduled point-in-time copies, so RPO equals the backup frequency.

Storage Gateway gives on-premises applications ongoing local access, through NFS, SMB, iSCSI or VTL, to data stored in AWS. DataSync is a transfer engine that moves data in bulk or on a schedule, with no ongoing local access.
Multi-AZ provides a synchronous standby for automatic failover; only the DB cluster variant is readable. Read replicas are asynchronous, readable copies for scaling reads and for manual promotion.

Aurora is a single-writer cluster (plus Global Database secondaries) with full MySQL or PostgreSQL compatibility. Aurora DSQL is a serverless, active-active distributed SQL service with strong multi-Region consistency and a narrower PostgreSQL feature set.

Both offer multi-Region active-active writes; MRSC global tables also provide strong consistency, like DSQL. Global tables keep DynamoDB's key-value model and access patterns, whereas DSQL offers relational SQL with transactions across tables.

Both separate compute from shared, log-structured storage with fast replicas. HorizonDB is PostgreSQL-only and in preview, without cross-Region replicas or customer-managed keys yet, while Aurora also supports MySQL and offers Global Database.
A GSI can use any partition key, can be added at any time and is eventually consistent. An LSI keeps the table's partition key, must be created with the table and supports strongly consistent reads.

Cosmos DB offers five tunable consistency levels and automatic indexing of every property. DynamoDB offers strong or eventual reads per request, explicit GSIs and LSIs, and MREC or MRSC global tables.
The Data Catalog stores the metadata (databases, tables, partitions). Lake Formation governs who can see which databases, tables, columns, rows and cells of it, through grants and LF-Tags.
CloudTrail records who called which API and when. CloudWatch records how resources and applications behave, through metrics, logs and alarms; AWS Config records how they are configured.
A metric filter turns matching log lines into a metric value. A subscription filter forwards the matching log events themselves to Lambda, Kinesis, Firehose or OpenSearch.

X-Ray is the trace store and console, plus legacy SDKs that are now in maintenance mode. ADOT is the vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry instrumentation that sends traces to X-Ray or elsewhere, and is the recommended path.

CloudWatch investigations is an assistant that you start from an alarm, metric or query, and it suggests telemetry and hypotheses for you to accept. DevOps Agent is an autonomous frontier agent that starts on alerts and correlates code, deployments and telemetry to propose a root cause and mitigation.
Secrets Manager charges per secret but offers rotation, cross-Region replication and resource policies. Parameter Store is free at the Standard tier and hierarchical, but has no built-in rotation.
Parameter Store holds values that applications read when they need them. AppConfig deploys configuration and feature flags gradually, with validators and automatic rollback on alarms.

A key policy is the key's permanent, mandatory access document. A grant is a programmatic, revocable delegation, often temporary, that works without editing the key policy; AWS services such as EBS use grants.

KMS is a multi-tenant, AWS-operated key service integrated with almost every AWS service. CloudHSM gives you dedicated HSMs in your VPC, where only you control the keys and crypto users, but it integrates with fewer services.

KMS keys are governed by mandatory key policies and never leave the service. Key Vault also stores secrets and certificates in the same vault and uses Azure RBAC, with Managed HSM for single-tenant keys.

Security Hub, generally available since December 2025, correlates findings into OCSF exposures with attack paths. Security Hub CSPM is the renamed original service, which runs Config-backed compliance controls and uses ASFF.
Security Hub correlates and prioritizes findings and automates routing. Security Incident Response triages them into cases, adds AWS CIRT responders and carries out pre-authorized containment.

Detective is an analyst tool for scoping an incident through a behavior graph. Security Incident Response is a managed process for triage, case management and containment, which can draw on Detective's evidence.
GuardDuty detects active threats from logs and runtime behaviour. Inspector finds vulnerabilities and exposure in EC2, container images, Lambda and code before they are exploited.

Defender for Cloud bundles CSPM and workload threat detection in one service. On AWS those jobs are split across Security Hub, Security Hub CSPM, GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie, so only the whole stack is close.

Azure Firewall Manager governs Azure Firewall, WAF and DDoS policies for hubs and VNets. Enforcing security groups and DNS firewall rules across an organization, as AWS Firewall Manager does, maps to Azure Policy instead.
A user pool authenticates users and issues JWTs for your APIs. An identity pool exchanges those tokens, or others, for temporary AWS credentials so the app can call AWS services directly.
Cognito user pools authenticate your application's customers. IAM Identity Center authenticates your workforce into AWS accounts and business applications through permission sets.
CDK is general-purpose IaC, written in programming languages, that synthesizes CloudFormation. SAM is a YAML extension of CloudFormation focused on serverless, with a CLI for local testing and sync.

Both let C# code drive cloud provisioning. CDK models infrastructure as constructs that synthesize CloudFormation for any workload, while Aspire models an application's resources and generates Bicep mainly for the services it hosts.

CloudFormation keeps explicit stack state, with change sets and rollback per stack. ARM deployments are idempotent against live resource state with what-if, and deployment stacks add lifecycle management.

Both host private NuGet, npm, PyPI and Maven feeds with upstream sources. CodeArtifact organizes feeds into domains with IAM resource policies, while Azure Artifacts scopes feeds to Azure DevOps organizations and projects.

Both provide Git-driven hosting with branch and pull-request preview environments. Amplify adds SSR hosting and CDK-based Gen 2 backends, while Static Web Apps pairs with managed Azure Functions APIs.

A billing alarm watches a single estimated-charges metric in us-east-1. Budgets track cost, usage, RI or Savings Plans against actual or forecast thresholds, by any filter, and can take budget actions.

Compute Optimizer generates rightsizing recommendations for resources. Cost Optimization Hub aggregates those and other recommendations across accounts, deduplicates them and estimates savings after your discounts.

Savings Plans commit to an hourly spend and, depending on the type, float across instance families, Regions or services. Reserved Instances commit to specific instance attributes and reserve capacity when zonal.
